item.title: Docs: Desktop environments
item.description:
This page explains how to install several desktop environments.

KDE Plasma

This command installs the KDE Plasma desktop environment.

1

$ sudo luet install layers/plasma apps/discover

The layers/plasma package ships with the SDDM login manager. If you prefer to use SDDM as your login manager run this command:

1

$ sudo systemctl enable sddm --force

GNOME

This command installs the GNOME desktop environment.

1

$ sudo luet install layers/gnome apps/gnome-software

The layers/gnome package ships with the GDM login manager. If you prefer to use GDM as your login manager run this command:

1

$ sudo systemctl enable gdm --force

MATE

This command installs the MATE desktop environment.

1

$ sudo luet install layers/mate themes/mate

XFCE

This command installs the XFCE desktop environment.

1

$ sudo luet install layers/xfce

LXQT

This command installs the LXQT desktop environment.

1

$ sudo luet install layers/lxqt

Cinnamon

This command installs the Cinnamon desktop environment.

1

$ sudo luet install layers/cinnamon

Enlightenment

This command installs the Enlightenment desktop environment.

1

$ sudo luet install layers/enlightenment

Trinity

This command installs the Trinity desktop environment.

1

$ sudo luet install layers/trinity

Hyprland

Hyprland is available in the community repository.

This command installs the Hyprland desktop environment.

1

$ sudo luet install layers/hyprland apps/kitty

Niri + Noctalia shell

Niri is a scrollable-tiling Wayland compositor.

This command installs Niri:

1

$ sudo luet install layers/niri

The following applications are required and available in the community repository:

1

$ sudo luet install apps/alacritty apps/fastfetch apps/noctalia

After installation, set up the Noctalia shell configuration:

First add the following to ~/.config/niri/config.kdl to disable Waybar and start Noctalia on login:

// spawn-at-startup "waybar"
spawn-at-startup "qs" "-c" "noctalia-shell"

Since noctalia version 5.0.x this should be:

// spawn-at-startup "waybar"
spawn-at-startup "noctalia"

Then install the Noctalia shell configuration to your user directory:

1
2
3

$ mkdir -p ~/.config/quickshell/noctalia-shell
$ curl -sL https://github.com/noctalia-dev/noctalia/releases/latest/download/noctalia-latest.tar.gz \
  | tar -xz --strip-components=1 -C ~/.config/quickshell/noctalia-shell

Log out and select Niri from your login manager’s session menu.

Notes

  • apps/alacritty is required as the default terminal (Super+T)
  • apps/noctalia provides the qs binary (Quickshell runtime)
  • The curl command installs the Noctalia shell config to your home directory; it is not managed by Luet and must be run once per user
  • apps/fastfetch is used by Noctalia for system info display

Fluxbox

This command installs the Fluxbox desktop environment.

1

$ sudo luet install layers/fluxbox

COSMIC

This command installs the COSMIC desktop environment.

1

$ sudo luet install layers/cosmic

Login managers

If you prefer to use Lightdm as your login manager run these commands:

1

$ sudo luet install apps/lightdm

1

$ sudo systemctl enable lightdm --force

If you prefer to use Slim as your login manager run these commands:

1

$ sudo luet install apps/slim

1

$ sudo systemctl enable slim --force

If you prefer to use Ly as your login manager run these commands:

1

$ sudo luet install apps/ly

1

$ sudo systemctl enable ly@tty2.service --force

Ly available in the community repository.

item.title: Docs: Gaming
item.description:
This page covers the main ways to play games on MocaccinoOS Desktop, from the Steam client to GOG and Epic games, and the tools that go with them.

Quick reference

Tool Used for Where it comes from Install
Steam Steam library, includes Gamemode and VKBasalt Desktop repository sudo luet install apps/steam
Epic Games Launcher Official Epic launcher for Linux (preview) Desktop repository sudo luet install apps/epic-games-launcher
Proton GE Custom Proton with extra patches Community repository sudo luet install apps/proton-ge-custom-bin
Heroic Games Launcher Epic Games Store and GOG Flatpak flatpak install flathub com.heroicgameslauncher.hgl
Lutris Game platform for non-Steam games Community repository sudo luet install apps/lutris
Nvidia drivers Proprietary Nvidia GPU drivers Desktop repository sudo luet install kernel-modules/nvidia-drivers-lts
MangoHud FPS and hardware overlay Community repository sudo luet install apps/mangohud

Proton GE, Lutris and MangoHud are in the community repository. Enable it first if you have not done so already.

Steam

We recommend installing Steam directly from the desktop repository:

$ sudo luet install apps/steam

You can also use the Flatpak version, but it runs in a sandbox, which can cause problems with some games.

Gamemode

Gamemode temporarily applies optimizations while a game is running. It is bundled in the apps/steam package, so it is installed together with Steam.

To start a game with Gamemode, right-click the game in your Library, select Properties… and enter this in the Launch Options box:

gamemoderun %command%

VKBasalt

VKBasalt is a post-processing layer for Vulkan that lets you enhance graphics further. It only works with Vulkan, which includes all Proton games. It is bundled in the apps/steam package, so it is installed together with Steam.

To use VKBasalt for a Steam game, enter this as a launch option:

ENABLE_VKBASALT=1 %command%

For non-Steam games, start the game from a terminal like this:

$ ENABLE_VKBASALT=1 mygame

Steam library on an NTFS partition

If you share a partition with Windows that holds a Steam library, games can fail to launch. Proton creates files and folders with names that are not valid on Windows, most commonly with a : (colon) in the name. NTFS cannot store these, which leads to disk errors.

The fix is to make the compatdata folder on the NTFS disk a symlink to a folder on a Linux partition.

First, if a compatdata folder already exists on the NTFS disk, remove it. The symlink cannot be created while it is there. It holds Proton prefixes (per-game Wine environments), so back up any game saves you need from it first.

Then create the folder on the Linux side and link to it from the NTFS disk (adjust the path to your mounted disk):

$ mkdir -p ~/.steam/steam/steamapps/compatdata
$ ln -s ~/.steam/steam/steamapps/compatdata /media/gamedisk/Steam/steamapps/

Proton GE

Proton GE is a fork of Valve’s Proton, made by GloriousEggroll (GE). This custom Proton version has several patches and bleeding-edge technology that can help increase performance.

Proton GE is in the community repository. With that repository enabled, install it with:

$ sudo luet install apps/proton-ge-custom-bin

Restart Steam afterwards. Proton GE then shows up in the compatibility settings.

Epic Games Launcher

The Epic Games Launcher for Linux is available on MocaccinoOS. It is currently in preview, so expect it to change. Install it with:

$ sudo luet install apps/epic-games-launcher

Heroic Games Launcher (below) remains an alternative for Epic Games Store and GOG games.

Heroic Games Launcher

For games from the Epic Games Store or GOG, we recommend Heroic Games Launcher. Install it using Flatpak:

$ flatpak install flathub com.heroicgameslauncher.hgl

Lutris

Lutris is an alternative game platform. It is in the community repository. With that repository enabled, install it with:

$ sudo luet install apps/lutris

Nvidia drivers

MocaccinoOS does not come with the proprietary Nvidia drivers pre-installed. If you need them, run:

$ sudo luet install kernel-modules/nvidia-drivers-lts

MangoHud

MangoHud is an overlay that shows FPS, temperatures, CPU/GPU load and more. It is in the community repository. With that repository enabled, install it with:

$ sudo luet install apps/mangohud

To show it in a Steam game, enter this as a launch option:

mangohud %command%

Tuning your system for games

The Performance page covers settings that matter for gaming:

  • a low-latency TCP profile for online games and voice chat
  • a higher vm.max_map_count, which some games need (DayZ requires 1048576)
  • optional sched_ext schedulers, such as scx_lavd, which is aimed at gaming and interactive use

References

  • https://github.com/ValveSoftware/Proton/wiki/Using-a-NTFS-disk-with-Linux-and-Windows#preventing-ntfs-read-errors
  • https://wiki.archlinux.org/title/Gamemode#Run_Steam_with_gamemode
  • https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1787799592

item.title: Docs: Printing
item.description:
Printing

Set up and manage printers on MocaccinoOS using CUPS.

CUPS (Common Unix Printing System) is pre-installed on MocaccinoOS, so you can start adding printers right away without any additional setup.

Adding a Printer via the CUPS Web Interface

CUPS includes a built-in web interface for managing printers.

Open the CUPS Web UI

Open your browser and navigate to:

http://localhost:631

Add a New Printer

Go to Administration → Add Printer. You may be prompted to authenticate — use your system username and password (your account must have administrator privileges).

CUPS will scan for available devices. Select your printer from the list, or choose the appropriate connection type manually if it is not detected automatically.

Configure the Printer

Fill in the printer details:

  • Name: a short identifier with no spaces (e.g. HP_OfficeJet)
  • Description: a human-friendly label (e.g. HP OfficeJet Pro 9015)
  • Location: optional, useful in shared environments (e.g. Office Room 2)

Click Continue.

Select a Driver

CUPS will suggest a driver based on the detected printer model. Accept the suggestion or browse the list to find the closest match. If your manufacturer provides a PPD file, you can upload it at this step for more accurate support.

Click Add Printer to confirm.

Set Default Options

Configure default printing options such as paper size, print quality, and duplex (double-sided) printing, then click Set Default Options.

Your printer is now ready to use.

Network & Shared Printers

MocaccinoOS supports printers connected directly to your network or shared by another computer.

Network Printer (IPP / AirPrint)

Most modern network printers support IPP (Internet Printing Protocol). To add one:

  1. Open the CUPS Web UI at http://localhost:631.
  2. Go to Administration → Add Printer.
  3. Select Internet Printing Protocol (IPP) as the connection type.
  4. Enter the printer URI in the Connection field:
ipp://<printer-ip-address>/ipp/print
  1. Complete the name, description, and driver selection as described above.

Printer Shared by Another Linux Machine (CUPS-to-CUPS)

If a printer is shared by another machine running CUPS on your network, it may be discovered automatically. Check under Discovered Network Printers when adding a new printer.

If it does not appear, add it manually using:

ipp://<host-ip>:631/printers/<printer-name>

Printer Shared by a Windows Machine (Samba / SMB)

To connect to a printer shared by a Windows PC:

  1. Select Windows Printer via SAMBA as the connection type.
  2. Enter the SMB URI:
smb://<host-ip>/<printer-name>
  1. If the shared printer requires authentication, enter the Windows username and password when prompted.
  2. Complete driver selection and configuration as usual.

Managing Printers

You can manage all installed printers from http://localhost:631 under the Printers tab. From there you can pause or resume a printer, set a default printer, view and cancel print jobs, modify printer options, or remove a printer.

Printing on KDE Plasma

KDE Plasma integrates with CUPS through the Print Manager tool, available in System Settings.

Open System Settings → Printers. You may be prompted to authenticate with your administrator password.

Click Add Printer. Plasma will scan for available printers on your system and network. Select your printer from the list and click Next. Plasma will suggest a driver — accept it or browse the list to find a better match. Give the printer a name and description, then click Finish.

To manage existing printers, print jobs, or set a default printer, return to System Settings → Printers at any time.

Printing on GNOME

GNOME handles printer setup directly from the Settings application.

Open the Activities overview and search for Printers, or go to Settings → Printers. Click Unlock in the top-right corner and authenticate with your administrator password.

Click the + button to add a printer. GNOME will display a list of detected printers — select yours and click Add. USB printers are often detected and added automatically as soon as they are connected.

To configure an existing printer, click the settings (⚙) button next to it. From there you can modify printer options, set it as the default, view active jobs, or remove it.

item.title: Docs: Network configuration
item.description:
Network configuration

MocaccinoOS uses Network Manager to manage network connections by default. It handles wired and wireless connections automatically and can be controlled via the nmcli command line tool, a graphical applet in your desktop environment, or the nmtui text interface.

For users who prefer a more minimal setup, systemd-networkd is also available as an alternative.

Network Manager

Checking status

To verify Network Manager is running and connected:

1

nmcli general status

To list all network interfaces and their state:

1

nmcli device status

To list all configured connection profiles:

1

nmcli connection show

Wi-Fi

Scan for available networks:

1

nmcli device wifi list

Connect to a network:

1

nmcli device wifi connect <SSID> password <password>

Disconnect from Wi-Fi:

1

nmcli device disconnect <interface>

To enable or disable Wi-Fi:

1
2

nmcli radio wifi on
nmcli radio wifi off

Wired (Ethernet)

Wired connections are configured automatically via DHCP when a cable is plugged in. If you need to set a static IP address on a connection, see the Static IP section below.

To bring a wired connection up or down manually:

1
2

nmcli connection up <connection-name>
nmcli connection down <connection-name>

Static IP

To assign a static IP address to an existing connection:

1

nmcli connection modify <connection-name> ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses 192.168.1.50/24 ipv4.gateway 192.168.1.1 ipv4.dns 192.168.1.1

Then bring the connection back up to apply the changes:

1

nmcli connection up <connection-name>

To revert back to DHCP:

1
2

nmcli connection modify <connection-name> ipv4.method auto
nmcli connection up <connection-name>

nmtui

If you prefer a simple text-based interface over the command line, Network Manager includes nmtui. Launch it with:

1

nmtui

This opens a menu-driven interface where you can add, edit, and activate connections without needing to remember nmcli syntax.

systemd-networkd

If you prefer to use systemd-networkd instead of Network Manager, follow the steps below.

1. Switch services

Disable Network Manager and enable systemd-networkd:

1
2
3

systemctl stop NetworkManager
systemctl disable NetworkManager
systemctl enable --now systemd-networkd

Then enable systemd-resolved for DNS resolution:

1

systemctl enable --now systemd-resolved

2. Find your interface name

Run networkctl to list available network interfaces:

1

networkctl

Example output:

IDX LINK    TYPE     OPERATIONAL SETUP
  1 lo      loopback carrier     unmanaged
  2 enp3s0  ether    routable    configured
  3 enp2s0  ether    off         unmanaged

Note the name of the interface you want to configure (e.g. enp3s0).

3. Configure your interface

Create a configuration file for your interface:

1

nano /etc/systemd/network/00-enp3s0.network

Static IP:

1
2
3
4
5
6
7

[Match]
Name=enp3s0

[Network]
Address=192.168.1.50/24
Gateway=192.168.1.1
DNS=192.168.1.1

DHCP:

1
2
3
4
5

[Match]
Name=enp3s0

[Network]
DHCP=yes

After saving the file, restart the service to apply your changes:

1

systemctl restart systemd-networkd

Firewall

MocaccinoOS includes the Linux kernel’s nftables firewall framework and the nft userspace utility. By default, no firewall rules are configured, allowing you to create a ruleset that matches your requirements.

A minimal configuration can be placed in /etc/nftables.conf:

#!/usr/sbin/nft -f

flush ruleset

table inet filter {
    chain input {
        type filter hook input priority 0;
        policy drop;

        # Allow loopback
        iif lo accept

        # Allow established and related connections
        ct state established,related accept

        # Drop invalid packets
        ct state invalid drop

        # Allow ICMP
        ip protocol icmp accept
        ip6 nexthdr ipv6-icmp accept

        # Allow SSH (optional)
        tcp dport 22 accept
    }

    chain forward {
        type filter hook forward priority 0;
        policy drop;
    }

    chain output {
        type filter hook output priority 0;
        policy accept;
    }
}

Enable the firewall at boot:

1

systemctl enable --now nftables

View the active ruleset:

1

nft list ruleset

Open additional services by adding the appropriate ports to the input chain. For example:

  • SSH: 22/tcp
  • HTTP: 80/tcp
  • HTTPS: 443/tcp
  • FTP: 21/tcp (plus the configured passive port range)
  • Samba: 445/tcp (and NetBIOS ports if required)

item.title: Docs: File sharing
item.description: File sharing is a critical aspect of modern computing, allowing systems to exchange files and access remote resources efficiently. In the Linux ecosystem, there are several powerful and versatile protocols, each suited for different use cases—from sharing files with Windows desktops to high-performance, native Linux networking, and secure remote access.

item.title: Docs: Internationalization
item.description:
MocaccinoOS provides optional internationalization features through modular layers. This includes input methods, language data, and fonts for non-Latin scripts.

These components are not installed by default to keep the base system minimal, but can be added at any time.

Available features

  • Input methods (Chinese, Japanese, Korean, etc.)
  • Fonts for additional scripts (CJK, emoji, etc.)
  • Locale and language data

All internationalization layers follow the MocaccinoOS design principle of including runtime components only, keeping the system lightweight.

item.title: Docs: Performance Optimizations
item.description:
MocaccinoOS ships with system and network optimizations for desktop responsiveness, gaming and low-latency networking. Most users do not need to change anything.

This page lists the default optimizations, explains how to customize them, and describes two optional features that are off by default.

Default optimizations

The defaults are set in /usr/lib/sysctl.d/70-mocaccino.conf.

Network

1
2

net.core.default_qdisc=fq
net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control=bbr

FQ (Fair Queuing) improves packet scheduling and reduces latency spikes under load. BBR improves latency consistency and throughput on modern broadband.

To verify the congestion control algorithm:

1

$ sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control

Memory

1
2
3
4
5
6

vm.swappiness=10
vm.dirty_background_ratio=3
vm.dirty_ratio=8
vm.dirty_expire_centisecs=1200
vm.dirty_writeback_centisecs=500
vm.vfs_cache_pressure=50
  • A low vm.swappiness keeps active applications in RAM instead of swapping them out.
  • The vm.dirty_* settings start writing buffered data to disk earlier and limit how much can build up. This smooths disk I/O and reduces micro-stutters, at the cost of slightly lower peak sequential write throughput.
  • A lower vm.vfs_cache_pressure keeps filesystem metadata cached longer, which helps games, development environments and large source trees.

Filesystem

1
2

fs.inotify.max_user_watches=524288
fs.inotify.max_user_instances=1024

These higher inotify limits prevent file monitoring errors in IDEs, Docker and game engines working with large projects.

Customizing settings

Changes to /usr/lib/sysctl.d/70-mocaccino.conf are overwritten on updates. Put your own settings in /etc/sysctl.d/99-custom.conf instead.

After changing the file, apply the settings:

1

$ sudo sysctl --system

To check a single setting:

1

$ sysctl <setting>

To restore the defaults, delete your custom file and reload:

1
2

$ sudo rm /etc/sysctl.d/99-custom.conf
$ sudo sysctl --system

TCP buffer sizes

Two example profiles are available. Use only one at a time.

For gaming, voice chat and video calls (favors latency over maximum throughput):

1
2
3
4

net.core.rmem_max=4194304
net.core.wmem_max=4194304
net.ipv4.tcp_rmem=4096 87380 4194304
net.ipv4.tcp_wmem=4096 16384 4194304

For file transfers, streaming and NAS (favors throughput):

1
2
3
4

net.core.rmem_max=16777216
net.core.wmem_max=16777216
net.ipv4.tcp_rmem=4096 87380 16777216
net.ipv4.tcp_wmem=4096 65536 16777216

vm.max_map_count

The default is 65530. Some applications need a higher limit, such as Elasticsearch, game engines, AI/ML workloads and certain modern games. For example, to set it to 262144:

1
2

$ echo "vm.max_map_count=262144" | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.d/99-custom.conf
$ sudo sysctl --system

Recommended values:

Use case Value
Default Linux 65530
Elasticsearch / databases 262144
High-performance workloads 1048576+

The game DayZ requires 10485761.

Optional: CPU-optimized graphics libraries

MocaccinoOS is built for the baseline x86-64 instruction set so it runs on every x86-64 CPU. The optional layers/X-v3 layer provides graphics and media libraries rebuilt for the x86-64-v3 level (AVX, AVX2, FMA, BMI1/BMI2), supported by Intel Haswell / AMD Excavator and newer CPUs (about 2013 and later).

The layer contains Mesa, Vulkan-loader, libepoxy, libglvnd, GLEW, FFmpeg and OpenAL. More libraries are planned. They are installed in /usr/lib64/glibc-hwcaps/x86-64-v3/.

glibc (2.33 and newer) checks at every process launch whether the CPU supports v3. If it does, the optimized libraries are used. If it does not, the normal system libraries are used. No configuration is needed, so installing the layer is safe on any CPU.

This command installs the layer:

1

$ sudo luet install layers/X-v3

The layer is not part of the graphical installer.

The expected gain is small:

  • Mesa, Vulkan-loader, libepoxy, libglvnd and GLEW mostly pass work between the game and the GPU driver. In GPU-bound scenarios, which is most gaming at higher resolutions, there is little room to matter. CPU-bound cases such as very high refresh-rate games or a weak CPU with a strong GPU may benefit slightly.
  • FFmpeg already uses hand-written SIMD code with runtime CPU detection for its main codecs, so the standard build already gets most of the AVX2 benefit.

One user comparing an x86-64-v3 Proton build to a standard build on capable AMD hardware measured no additional FPS2. If you notice no difference, that is an expected result, not a bug.

Optional: sched_ext schedulers

The CPU scheduler decides which program runs on which core, and when. Linux uses EEVDF by default. sched_ext (kernel 6.12 and newer) lets you load an alternative scheduler while the system is running, without a reboot or a kernel rebuild.

The Stable and LTS kernels ship with sched_ext enabled. Nothing changes until you load a scheduler yourself. If the kernel detects a scheduling problem, it falls back to the default scheduler automatically3.

Enabling sched_ext requires a few supporting kernel options (BTF type information, function tracing hooks and some BPF settings). This adds a few megabytes of type information to the kernel for everyone. The tracing hooks should have a negligible effect when tracing is not in use.

Update to the latest kernel, reboot, and install the schedulers:

1

$ sudo luet install apps/scx

Start a scheduler from a terminal:

1

$ sudo scx_lavd

To check that it is active, run this in another terminal:

1
2
3

$ cat /sys/kernel/sched_ext/state
enabled
$ cat /sys/kernel/sched_ext/root/ops

Press Ctrl+C to stop the scheduler and return to the default one. A scheduler started this way also stops at reboot.

scx_lavd (aimed at gaming and interactive use) and scx_bpfland (aimed at low response times) have been verified to load and run on MocaccinoOS kernels. Other schedulers from the scx project have not been tried, and none have been benchmarked on MocaccinoOS yet.

Results depend on the workload:

  • The scx_lavd developers report higher frame rates, fewer stutters and slightly lower power use in games3. This is their measurement on their workloads.
  • In a third-party benchmark (June 2026) of compiling and stress tests, EEVDF was essentially tied for fastest, while scx_lavd took roughly 8% longer in total4. Schedulers tuned for low latency may give up some raw throughput.
  • In GPU-bound games, the CPU scheduler has little room to matter.

If a scheduler does not help your workload, stop it and carry on with the default.

  1. https://steamcommunity.com/app/221100/discussions/0/3199241400256965913/#c3199241400263431941 ↩︎

  2. https://forums.linuxmint.com/viewtopic.php?t=457800 ↩︎

  3. https://lwn.net/Articles/991205/ ↩︎

  4. https://reddit.sentinel-team.org/posts/1u5uf16/snapshots/2026-06-19T21%3A03%3A49.564114Z ↩︎

item.title: Docs: Development guidelines
item.description:
This documentation section tries to summarize and provide general guidelines while applying changes to MocaccinoOS Desktop.

A prior knowledge of the basics of how to build packages with luet is assumed, it’s strongly advised to follow the Getting started docs of Luet before going ahead.
